periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Before Reading: Bravery, Soldiers, and the Battle Ahead

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.49): paired discussion on Republic Day Parade and bravery awards.
Let us read (p.49): group discussion on qualities a soldier should have.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick paired exchange on the Republic Day Parade — what students know about it and the awards given on the day. Draw out prior knowledge warmly without correcting or grading responses.

Move to the group-of-four discussion: what qualities should a soldier have, and what message would students send to a soldier? Circulate and prompt quieter voices; take brief notes on the board of ideas that emerge.

Teacher reads aloud the opening pages of the prose section (p.49–54), with students following in their textbooks. Pause at the description of Operation Gulmarg and Major Sharma's insistence on leading despite his plastered hand — invite a brief verbal reaction.
Close with a short whole-class share-out: what one word would each student use to describe the kind of officer Major Sharma appears to be so far, and why? Accept responses orally; no written task.

periods.teacher_notes: The before-reading discussions are the pedagogical entry point into the tribute narrative; they surface students' schema about soldiers and civic duty before the text shapes it. Watch for students who conflate ceremonial bravery with battlefield courage — the section's account of Badgam will complicate both ideas productively. Students who are reluctant to speak should be invited with open, low-stakes prompts rather than direct nomination.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for noting student ideas

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Reading the Battle: Chronology and Close Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.59): arrange eight events in chronological order.
Let us think and reflect (p.59–60): Extract 1 — inference MCQ, fill-in, and assertion-reason.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the battle account on p.55–58, students following. Pause briefly at Sharma's legendary last words so students can absorb them before moving to tasks.

Students work in pairs on the chronological ordering task at p.59 — eight events to arrange, with the first and last already marked. After pairs confer, build the correct sequence on the board through class discussion, asking students to justify each placement using the text.

Guide the class through Extract 1 (p.59–60): read the extract aloud, then work through the inference MCQ, the assertion-reason MCQ, and the fill-in-blank item together. Elicit reasoning for each answer rather than accepting bare choices.

Students independently write their answer to the sentence-completion item ('Despite heavy casualties…because ________') in their notebooks. Take two or three volunteers to share; highlight the variety in phrasing.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the account of D Company's stand at Badgam, students should now be able to trace the sequence of Sharma's decisions with textual evidence. A common difficulty at this stage is treating assertion-reason items as ordinary MCQs — pause to explain the logical structure before the class attempts the item. The open ECR questions in Part II of the same exercise are rich but time-intensive; they are flagged for self-study or a future extended discussion rather than class time here.
materials: Blackboard for building the chronological sequence

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Early Life and Legacy: Extract Analysis and Reflective Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.60–61): Extract 2 — inference MCQ, true/false, and short-answer items.
Let us think and reflect (p.61): two ECR questions on Sharma's legacy and last words.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.61): write short paragraphs on the remaining ECR questions about Sharma's inspiration today.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 2 (p.60–61) aloud — Sharma's early life in Kangra, his family legacy, Sherwood College, and Sandhurst. Students follow in their books.

Work through Extract 2 tasks (p.60–61) in a teacher-led discussion: the inference MCQ on early influences, the true/false statement on family wealth, and the short-answer on 'served the nation with distinction.' Ask students to point to specific lines in the extract that support each answer.

Shift to the reflective Part II questions (p.61): discuss in class the significance of the phrase 'forever alive, forever alive' and why Sharma's leadership was critical at Badgam. Elicit multiple perspectives; push students to move beyond plot summary toward reasoned argument.

Students write a response in their notebooks to one of the two ECR questions discussed, aiming for three to four sentences with a clear claim and textual support. The remaining ECR questions from the same section are set as independent written work to be completed at home.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read both the battle account and Sharma's early life, students are equipped to connect his family background and military training to the conduct he showed at Badgam. A common pitfall when discussing legacy questions is vague, inspirational language — push students to ground every claim in a specific act or decision from the narrative. The phrase-replacement item in Extract 2 (finding a synonym for the underlined phrase) is best handled by directing students to re-read the surrounding sentences for contextual clues.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Listening to the Param Vir Chakra: Fill-in-Blank Accuracy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.66): fill five blanks with exact words or phrases from the Param Vir Chakra talk.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening task: explain that students will hear a short talk about the Param Vir Chakra and must capture specific words and phrases in five blanks. Distribute or direct students to the blanks on p.66, and allow a moment to read the incomplete sentences before the first reading.
Read the transcript aloud at natural pace (first reading). Students listen without writing. After the first reading, give students a brief pause to recall what they heard.
Read the transcript aloud a second time, slightly more slowly. Students fill in the blanks as they listen. Emphasise that they need exact words or short phrases from the talk.

Class verification: go through each blank in order, asking volunteers to share their answer. Write the correct answers on the board. Discuss any blank where students heard differently — connect the answer back to the specific sentence in the talk.

Brief consolidation discussion: what additional detail in the talk surprised students or was new to them about the Param Vir Chakra's design and history? Accept three or four oral responses without written follow-up.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript describes the Param Vir Chakra's symbolism, its institution by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, and Mrs. Savitri Khanolkar's design drawing on the Vedic rishi Dadhichi — details students may not encounter elsewhere in the chapter. A common difficulty in fill-in tasks is paraphrasing instead of using exact wording; remind students before the second reading that precision matters here. Students who mishear a term — for example 'Vedic rishi' — benefit from seeing the correct form on the board alongside a brief explanation.
materials: Teacher's copy of the listening transcript (p.98)

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Speaking on Duty; Planning a Formal Letter of Enquiry

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.66–67): group talk on serving the nation — choose a theme and use sentence prompts.
Let us write (p.67–68): study the letter-of-enquiry format and plan key content before drafting.

homework.task_brief: Let us write (p.67–68): complete a fair-copy draft of the letter of enquiry using notes from the planning phase.

time_bands.activity: Frame the speaking task: citizens of a nation fulfill duty in many ways — not only on the battlefield. Briefly name the four themes available (environment, health, helping others, righteous conduct) and let groups of four to five students choose their theme.

Groups confer using the sentence prompts on p.66–67 to organise their thinking. Each group selects a speaker to present to the class. Presenters speak; the teacher notes one strength and one suggestion per group on the board after each turn.

Transition to writing: teacher reads aloud the letter-of-enquiry task on p.67–68 and displays the formal letter layout. Work through each structural element — sender's address, date, subject line, body paragraphs, closing — and note the four content points students must cover (visit dates, duration, entry fees, student guidelines).

Students draft a rough plan: headings for each paragraph with two or three key phrases or cues. Teacher circulates to check that the four required content points appear and that the register stays formal. Address common errors in salutation and subject line on the board.
Wrap up: students are asked to write a clean draft of the full letter using their plan. Note that peer review of register and layout will benefit the draft before it is finalised.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking task draws on the same values-of-duty theme that runs through the tribute narrative, giving the oral work genuine thematic coherence with the text. In the writing segment, the most common structural error for Grade VIII students writing formal letters is omitting or misplacing the subject line — model its position clearly before students plan. The full drafted letter is set as independent follow-up work so that drafting, not just planning, reaches completion.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Battlefield Idioms, Collective Nouns, and 'Over-' Verbs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.62): match battlefield idioms to situations; complete sentences with idioms.
Let us learn (p.62–63): match collective nouns for armed forces; fill blanks with correct term.
Let us learn (p.64): fill blanks distinguishing overwhelm/overthrow/overrun from definitions.

time_bands.activity: Present the four battlefield idioms — fight to the last man, foil the plan, deliver a blow, hold their ground — as they appear in the prose section. Students match each to the four situations on p.62 individually, then pairs compare answers before class verification. Follow immediately with the four sentence-completion items using the same idioms.

Introduce the collective nouns for armed forces (regiment, squadron, fleet, battalion) on p.62–63. Students work individually on the match task, then complete the four fill-in-blank sentences. Class verification on the board — emphasise the structural logic: air force uses squadron, navy uses fleet, army uses regiment and battalion.

Teacher presents the three 'over-' verbs (overwhelm, overthrow, overrun) with their definitions on p.64. Students fill in the three definition blanks. Then, in pairs, students brainstorm at least three more 'over-' verbs and frame one sentence each — share two or three aloud.

Quick whole-class consolidation: teacher calls out a situation (e.g., 'Enemy troops flood into a town') and students supply the correct 'over-' verb or battlefield idiom. Run four to five rapid-fire rounds to end the unit on an energetic note.

periods.teacher_notes: The idioms in this unit are drawn directly from the prose account of D Company's stand — connecting lexical items to the narrative context where students first met them strengthens retention. A common confusion is between 'overthrow' (remove from power) and 'overrun' (invade in numbers); the definitions task makes the distinction explicit, and the rapid-fire consolidation at the close tests whether students have internalised it. The noun-verb spelling pairs (advice/advise, etc.) and subject-verb agreement exercises are substantive tasks held for the dedicated grammar unit that follows.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Grammar in Context and Exploring Gallantry and Service

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.64): fill blanks choosing correct noun/verb form (advice/advise, practice/practise, etc.).
Let us learn (p.65–66): subject-verb agreement fill-in and passage correction.
Let us explore (p.68–69): read about Captain Vikram Batra; introduce gallantry awards research project.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.69): begin independent research on India's gallantry awards and women's roles in the Armed Forces.

time_bands.activity: Address the noun-verb spelling pairs on p.64 — advice/advise, practice/practise, device/devise, council/counsel. Teacher models the rule (nouns use 'c', verbs use 's') with one example, then students complete the four fill-in items. Verify on the board; note the British spelling 'defence' versus American 'defense' as a bonus observation.

Move to subject-verb agreement on p.65–66. Students attempt the ten fill-in-blank sentences individually. Class verification follows, with the teacher pausing on items involving collective phrases, 'neither…nor' constructions, and 'each of the…' — explaining the grammatical rule behind each. Students then correct the passage on p.66, identifying which verbs are wrong and supplying the right form.

Teacher reads the passage about Captain Vikram Batra on p.68–69 aloud. Brief discussion: what connects his story to Major Sharma's — what common thread runs through all twenty-one Param Vir Chakra recipients? Students share two or three observations orally.

Introduce the research project for the Let us explore section (p.69): students are to find information about India's gallantry award hierarchy and the key roles women play in the Indian Armed Forces, and prepare to share findings. Discuss where reliable sources might be found. The research itself is conducted independently outside class.

periods.teacher_notes: The noun-verb spelling distinction (c for nouns, s for verbs) is a rule students often know in isolation but misapply when embedded in a sentence — the fill-in format here forces them to read context carefully. Subject-verb agreement with 'neither…nor' and collective noun phrases is a recurring error in student writing at this stage; the passage correction task makes errors visible and correctable rather than abstract. The beyond-text project is launched here so students can begin research independently; findings will be shared in the synthesis unit.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Valour, Language, and Lasting Legacy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.61): oral discussion of Sharma's last words, legacy, and civic relevance.
Let us speak (p.66–67): selected students present their nation-service group talk to the whole class.
Let us explore (p.69): share patriotic songs from any language or region; connect to the chapter's themes.

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-class reflective discussion anchored in the prose tribute: revisit Sharma's last words ('I shall not withdraw an inch') and the repetition of 'forever alive, forever alive' from the closing lines. Ask students how the chapter defines courage — is it the absence of fear or something else? Draw on the text's account of the battle and his early life to ground responses.

Two or three groups deliver their oral presentations on how citizens can serve the nation, using their chosen theme from the Let us speak task. After each presentation, the class identifies one specific connection between the group's theme and Major Sharma's story — this cross-referencing move is the synthesis work.

Students share patriotic songs they know — in any language, including regional languages — naming the song, language, and one line they find particularly powerful. The teacher draws a brief connection between musical expressions of patriotism and the literary expression of valour in the chapter's tribute prose.

Closing synthesis: teacher maps on the board the chapter's main threads — the battle narrative, the vocabulary of military service, the formal letter of enquiry, the grammar of agreement, and the gallantry award tradition — and asks students: what single idea ties all of these together? Accept three to four responses and close without grading, leaving the question genuinely open.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together everything the chapter has taught — the narrative of Badgam, the language work on idioms and collective nouns, the formal writing register, and the broader tradition of gallantry awards and civic duty. Where students reference research on gallantry awards or women's roles in the Armed Forces, welcome those contributions; where they have not done the research, the class discussion and oral presentations carry the synthesis on their own. The board map at the close is a teacher act, not a student product, so it requires nothing prepared in advance.

items.source_lo: Student reads and interprets an informational prose tribute, sequencing events and drawing inferences about character, motivation, and legacy using the prose as the vehicle.

items.item_stem:
Arrange the following events from Major Somnath Sharma's life in the correct chronological order by numbering them 1 to 4, where 1 is the earliest.

(A) D Company was airlifted to Srinagar on 31 October 1947.
(B) Major Sharma attended the Royal Military College, Sandhurst.
(C) Major Sharma was awarded the Param Vir Chakra posthumously.
(D) Pakistan launched Operation Gulmarg to capture the Kashmir Valley.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. B (Sandhurst training preceded 1947), 2. D (Operation Gulmarg triggered the crisis), 3. A (D Company's airlift on 31 October 1947), 4. C (Param Vir Chakra awarded posthumously after the battle).

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student reads and interprets an informational prose tribute, sequencing events and drawing inferences about character, motivation, and legacy using the prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Operation Gulmarg, D Company's stand at Badgam, Sharma's last words, his early life in Kangra, Param Vir Chakra citation, National War Memorial Honour Wall.
items.item_stem: When ordered to withdraw at Badgam, Major Somnath Sharma refused, saying the enemy was only fifty yards away, that his company was heavily outnumbered, and that he would fight to the last man and the last round. What does this response reveal about Sharma's understanding of his role as a commander? Support your answer with evidence from the tribute narrative.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sharma's refusal to withdraw reveals that he understood his role as holding ground at any personal cost to buy time for reinforcements — not mere obedience to orders but a deliberate tactical and moral choice. His words show he prioritised the mission and his men's collective resolve over his own survival, which the narrative confirms when it notes that even after his death his company held the position for six more hours.

items.item_stem:
After listening to the talk about the Param Vir Chakra, answer the following question in one or two sentences:

The talk says the Param Vir Chakra's design draws on the Vedic rishi Sage Dadhichi. Based on what you heard, who commissioned this design, and what two symbolic elements appear around the State Emblem at the medal's centre?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The design was created by Mrs. Savitri Khanolkar. The two symbolic elements surrounding the State Emblem are four replicas of Indra's Vajra and lotus flowers.

items.item_stem: In a group of four to five students, choose one of the following themes — saving the environment, health and well-being, helping others, or righteous conduct — and present a two-to-three minute talk explaining how young citizens can serve their nation through that theme. Organise your talk with a clear opening, two or three specific ideas, and a closing statement that connects your theme to the spirit of duty the chapter describes.

expected_elements: Clear choice of one theme stated at the opening.
Two or three specific, actionable ideas linked to the theme.
Closing statement connects the theme to duty or service.
Register is confident and audience-aware throughout.

items.item_stem: Major Somnath Sharma's last words — 'I shall not withdraw an inch but will fight to the last man and the last round' — express an extreme form of duty and self-sacrifice. In a brief individual talk of one to two minutes, share your opinion: should ordinary citizens be expected to show the same kind of unconditional commitment to a cause, or is this a standard only for soldiers? Give at least one clear reason for your view.

expected_elements: A clearly stated opinion on unconditional civic duty.
At least one reasoned argument supporting the view.
Reference to Sharma's conduct or the chapter's values.
Confident, appropriate register for a class discussion.

items.item_stem: Your school wishes to organise a visit to the National War Memorial in New Delhi. As the student secretary of your school, write a formal letter of enquiry to the Memorial's Incharge. Your letter must request information on the following: (a) dates available for school group visits, (b) the duration of a guided tour, (c) any entry fees for student groups, and (d) specific guidelines students must follow during the visit. Use a formal letter layout with all required structural elements.

expected_elements: Correct formal letter layout: sender's address, date, subject line, salutation, body, closing.
All four content points addressed clearly in the body.
Formal, polite register maintained throughout.
Correct grammar, punctuation, and paragraph organisation.

items.item_stem: The chapter describes Major Somnath Sharma's name inscribed on the National War Memorial's Honour Wall. Imagine you visited the Memorial and were deeply moved by what you saw. Write a personal letter to a friend describing your experience — what you saw, how you felt, and what you think young Indians should take away from a visit to such a memorial. Your letter should be written in a warm, personal register and should refer to at least one specific detail from the chapter about Major Sharma's story.

expected_elements: Informal personal letter format with appropriate salutation and closing.
Vivid description of the visit experience with at least one specific detail.
Reference to Major Sharma or the Honour Wall drawn from the chapter.
A personal reflection on what the visit means for young Indians.

squadron|a large infantry unit typically commanded by a lieutenant colonel
fleet|a small unit of twelve to twenty-four aircraft and their crews
regiment|a permanent army unit divided into several companies

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student applies vocabulary and grammar concepts drawn from the section's military and civic language — idioms, collective nouns, 'over-' verbs, noun-verb spelling pairs, and subject-verb agreement — using the prose context as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Battlefield idioms (fight to the last man, foil the plan, deliver a blow, hold their ground), collective nouns for armed forces (regiment, squadron, fleet, battalion), over- verbs, advice/advise noun-verb pairs, subject-verb agreement with collective and correlative constructions.
items.item_stem: The chapter describes how D Company chose to hold their ground at Badgam rather than withdraw. Using the battlefield idiom 'hold their ground' and one of the following 'over-' verbs — overwhelm, overrun, or overthrow — write two sentences of your own that together describe a situation in which a small but determined group resists a much larger force. Your sentences must show that you understand the precise meaning of both the idiom and the 'over-' verb you choose.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any two sentences that correctly use 'hold their ground' to mean standing firm without retreating, and that correctly use the chosen 'over-' verb — 'overrun' meaning invaded in large numbers, 'overwhelm' meaning flooded or overpowered, or 'overthrow' meaning removed from power. Both words must be used accurately in context, not simply inserted.

items.source_lo: Student investigates gallantry awards and the roles of women in the Indian Armed Forces through independent research and oral sharing, using the chapter's tribute context as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Twenty-one Param Vir Chakra awardees from Major Somnath Sharma to Captain Vikram Batra; gallantry award hierarchy; women's key roles in the Indian Armed Forces; patriotic songs across languages.
items.item_stem: The chapter introduces the Param Vir Chakra as India's highest gallantry award and notes that twenty-one recipients have received it, from Major Somnath Sharma to Captain Vikram Batra. Research and write a short note (one paragraph) about India's gallantry award hierarchy — naming at least three awards in order of precedence — and explain what criteria distinguish the Param Vir Chakra from the awards below it.

expected_elements: At least three gallantry awards named in correct order of precedence.
Clear explanation of what makes the Param Vir Chakra distinct.
Reference to 'exemplary bravery in the presence of the enemy' criterion.
Paragraph is well-organised with a clear topic sentence.

items.item_stem: The chapter notes that the Indian government has worked to increase the representation of women in the Armed Forces. Design a short informational project (a poster plan, a structured set of notes, or a brief written report) that covers: (a) at least two key roles women currently hold in the Indian Army, Navy, or Air Force; (b) one milestone in the expansion of women's participation in the Armed Forces; and (c) your own reflection on why this expansion matters for the nation. Your project should be grounded in research and presented in a format a classmate could read and learn from.

expected_elements: At least two specific roles for women in the Armed Forces named accurately.
One concrete milestone in women's participation clearly stated.
A personal reflection that goes beyond a general statement.
Information is organised clearly and suited to sharing with peers.
